analysis.one_liner: Directs Treasury to list and break up banks and financial firms too big to fail.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it died in the Senate Banking Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury Department to publish, within 90 days, a list of any commercial banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies whose failure could wreck the US or global economy without a taxpayer bailout. One year later, Treasury would have to break those firms up into pieces small enough to fail without endangering the financial system. It was aimed at ending the expectation that the government must rescue giant financial firms with public money.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and depositors, who would no longer be on the hook to bail out financial giants whose collapse threatens the whole economy. Small and mid-sized banks would also benefit from competing against smaller rivals. Households hurt by the 2008 crisis and its bailouts were the intended constituency.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Treasury to publish a list of every commercial bank, investment bank, hedge fund, and insurance company it believes is too big to fail, within 90 days of enactment.
Beginning one year after enactment, Treasury must break up every listed entity so its failure would no longer cause a catastrophic effect on the US or global economy without a taxpayer bailout.
Defines too big to fail as any entity so large that its failure would catastatically destabilize the financial system or the US economy without substantial government assistance.

analysis.who_pays: The largest banks, investment banks, hedge funds, and insurance companies, which would be broken up and lose the scale advantages and the implicit government guarantee that comes with being too big to fail. Shareholders and executives of those firms would bear the restructuring costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: The largest Wall Street banks and insurers

drawbacks.text: Forcing Treasury to break up firms within one year, based on its own judgment, is a blunt mandate: the bill gives no criteria beyond a 'catastrophic effect' standard and no process for appeal, which critics could fairly call an unprecedented grant of unilateral power over private companies.

Breaking up the largest banks could raise costs for some large corporate customers and, at least in the transition, push some financial activity toward less-regulated foreign institutions, an objection supporters of big banks raised during the broader 2010 debate.
The one-year deadline left little time for orderly separations of firms that had spent decades consolidating, raising legal and market-disruption risks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — that no private firm should be so big its collapse forces taxpayers to bail it out — addresses a real, costly problem exposed by 2008. The costs fall on a concentrated industry rather than the public. The bill's weakness is design, not aim: a one-year, unilateral breakup mandate is far cruder than phased size caps or capital surcharges, and that bluntness gave opponents an easy argument. Still, nothing in the record suggests Congress ever weighed that trade-off; the bill never even got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on November 5, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The committee took no further action recorded in the bill's history: no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill died at the end of the 111th Congress without ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest banks, hedge funds, and insurers stayed whole: with no cosponsors and no committee action, the threat of a forced breakup never advanced. Six months later Congress enacted the Dodd-Frank Act, which created resolution procedures for failing giants but left the biggest firms' size intact, so the industry's concentrated structure survived this challenge.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Christopher Dodd (D-CT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: Partisan shape is hard to read from the record since no votes occurred, but zero cosponsors in a Senate with 58 Democrats and 1 Independent besides Sanders means no senator from any party joined him.

industries.note: Would have been listed and broken up within a year, losing both their scale advantages and the implicit taxpayer backstop that lets them borrow more cheaply. Their interest in avoiding the bill ran against taxpayers, who bear bailout costs.
Firms whose failure would threaten the financial system would have been dismantled rather than rescued at public expense.
Insurance giants whose collapse would require government assistance would have been included on the breakup list.
Smaller rivals of the megabanks would gain competitive ground if their largest competitors were broken apart; their interests track the bill's pro-depositor aims.
